about: Mechanics (AERO40007) is a core 7.5-credit Autumn-term module in Year 1 of Imperial's MEng Aeronautical Engineering (H401), according to the 2026–27 programme specification. It lays the classical mechanics foundation (statics, kinematics and dynamics) that later structures, dynamics and flight mechanics modules build on, running from vectors and moments of inertia through statics, virtual work, particle dynamics and vibrations to orbital mechanics. The topic titles and their order follow the department's module descriptor (the descriptor page could not be reloaded to re-check them for 2026–27). Reading 'Variational mechanics' as virtual work and potential-energy stability, and 'Simple motion' as particle kinematics, is this pack's interpretation of those titles, so check it against your lecture notes. The module-level assessment breakdown is not confirmed here.

notes.h: Vectors, moments and moments of inertia
notes.body:
Almost everything in this module is written in vector form, so fluent vector algebra is the first skill to secure. A vector has magnitude and direction and is written in components, e.g. a = (aₓ, a_y, a_z) in a right-handed Cartesian frame.

Dot (scalar) product:
- a·b = |a||b|cos θ = aₓbₓ + a_yb_y + a_zb_z.
- Uses: the angle between two directions, the component of a force along a line (F·n with n a unit vector), and work (F·dr).

Cross (vector) product:
- |a × b| = |a||b|sin θ, direction given by the right-hand rule, perpendicular to both a and b.
- Components: a × b = (a_yb_z − a_zb_y, a_zbₓ − aₓb_z, aₓb_y − a_ybₓ).
- Order matters: b × a = −(a × b).

Moment of a force:
- About a point O: M_O = r × F, where r runs from O to any point on the line of action of F (sliding the force along its line does not change the moment).
- About an axis through O with unit vector n: M_n = n·(r × F), a scalar.
- A couple (two equal, opposite, non-collinear forces) has the same moment about every point.

Worked example: F = (2, −1, 3) N acts at r = (1, 2, 0) m from O. Then M_O = (2×3 − 0×(−1), 0×2 − 1×3, 1×(−1) − 2×2) = (6, −3, −5) N m, with magnitude √(36 + 9 + 25) = √70 ≈ 8.37 N m.

Centre of mass: r_G = Σmᵢrᵢ / Σmᵢ (or ∫r dm / m for a continuous body). For a uniform body it coincides with the centroid.

Moment of inertia about an axis: I = Σmᵢrᵢ² = ∫r² dm, where r is the perpendicular distance from the axis. It measures resistance to angular acceleration about that axis, just as mass resists linear acceleration. The radius of gyration k is defined by I = mk².

Standard results (uniform bodies):
- Slender rod, length L, axis perpendicular to the rod: mL²/12 through the centre, mL²/3 through one end.
- Thin ring or hoop about its axis: mR².
- Solid disc or cylinder about its axis: mR²/2.
- Solid sphere about a diameter: 2mR²/5.
- Rectangular plate a × b about the axis through its centre perpendicular to the plate: m(a² + b²)/12.

Parallel axis theorem: I = I_G + md², where I_G is about an axis through the centre of mass and d is the distance to the parallel axis. It only works when one of the two axes passes through G. Example: rod about its end, I = mL²/12 + m(L/2)² = mL²/3.

Perpendicular axis theorem (plane laminae only): I_z = Iₓ + I_y, with x and y in the plane and z normal to it.

In three dimensions the inertia of a rigid body is described by a 3 × 3 inertia tensor whose diagonal terms are moments of inertia and whose off-diagonal terms involve the products of inertia (such as ∫xy dm). Axes for which the products of inertia vanish are principal axes; for symmetric bodies they lie along the symmetry axes. Sign conventions for the off-diagonal terms differ between textbooks, so follow the one used in your lecture notes.

Exam tips: always state the axis when quoting I; use the parallel axis theorem only from the axis through G; and check the order of a cross product, because reversing it flips the sign of every component.

notes.h: Equilibrium in three dimensions and dry friction
notes.body:
Statics asks when a body stays at rest (or moves at constant velocity) and what forces the supports must supply. The method is always the same: isolate the body, draw a free body diagram (FBD), then write the equilibrium equations.

Equilibrium conditions:
- Particle: ΣF = 0, which gives three scalar equations in 3D (two in 2D).
- Rigid body: ΣF = 0 and ΣM_O = 0 about any point O. That gives six scalar equations in 3D (three in 2D).
- If the number of unknown reactions equals the number of independent equations and the supports properly restrain the body, it is statically determinate. More unknowns means it is statically indeterminate and needs deformation (compatibility) information.

Writing 3D forces as vectors:
- A cable from A to B pulling on the body at A has force T = T(r_B − r_A)/|r_B − r_A|, i.e. tension times the unit vector along the cable.
- Take moments about a line through two unknown reactions to remove them from the equation; this often gives one unknown directly.

Typical 3D supports (follow the conventions in your notes):
- Ball-and-socket joint: three force components, no moment.
- Cable or light strut: one force along its own line.
- Fixed (built-in) support: three force components and three moment components.
- A two-force member (loaded only at two pins) carries a force along the line joining the pins. A body acted on by three non-parallel forces is in equilibrium only if their lines of action meet at one point.

Dry (Coulomb) friction:
- Before slipping, the friction force F is whatever is needed for equilibrium, up to a limit: F ≤ μ_s N.
- At impending slip, F = μ_s N, directed to oppose the motion that would occur.
- Once sliding, F = μ_k N, opposing the relative velocity; usually μ_k < μ_s.
- Angle of friction φ: tan φ = μ_s. A block on an incline of angle θ is on the point of slipping when tan θ = μ_s.

Worked example: a 50 kg crate sits on a 20° slope with μ_s = 0.4. Normal force N = mg cos 20° = 461 N, so maximum friction is 0.4 × 461 = 184 N. The friction needed to hold it is mg sin 20° = 168 N, which is less, so it stays put (equivalently tan 20° = 0.364 < 0.4). To start it moving up the slope with a force P parallel to the slope, friction now acts down the slope: P = mg(sin θ + μ_s cos θ) = 490.5 × (0.342 + 0.376) ≈ 352 N.

Tipping versus sliding: for a tall object pushed sideways, check both possibilities. It slides if the push exceeds μ_s N first; it tips if the normal reaction moves to the edge of the base first.

Belt and rope friction (capstan equation): for a rope on the point of slipping round a fixed drum, T₂/T₁ = e^(μβ), where T₂ is the tight-side tension and β is the wrap angle in radians. Tension ratio grows exponentially with wrap angle, which is why a few turns of rope round a bollard can hold a ship.

Exam tips: draw one FBD per body; show friction in the direction that opposes impending motion; state whether you are at impending slip (F = μN) or just in equilibrium (F ≤ μN); and in 3D, choose moment axes that remove as many unknowns as possible.

notes.h: Variational mechanics: virtual work and stability
notes.body:
Interpretation: the module descriptor gives this topic only the title 'Variational mechanics'. This note takes it to mean the principle of virtual work and potential-energy stability, the usual first-year treatment; your lectures may go further (for example to Lagrange's equations), so check your notes.

Variational (energy) methods treat equilibrium through work and energy rather than by balancing every force vector. Their great advantage is that forces at ideal supports and connections drop out, so mechanisms with several linked parts can be solved in a few lines.

Key definitions:
- Degrees of freedom: the number of independent coordinates needed to fix the configuration. Those coordinates (an angle θ, a length x) are generalised coordinates.
- Virtual displacement δq: an imagined, infinitesimal change of configuration that respects the constraints (it does not break pins or lift bodies off smooth surfaces) and happens with time frozen.
- Virtual work: δW = ΣF·δr, the work forces would do during the virtual displacement.

Principle of virtual work: a system whose constraints are ideal (they do no work, such as frictionless pins, smooth contacts and inextensible links) is in equilibrium if and only if the total virtual work of the applied forces is zero for every admissible virtual displacement. For one degree of freedom, δW = Q δq, so equilibrium requires the generalised force Q = 0.

Method:
- Choose a generalised coordinate (say θ).
- Write the position of each point where an applied force acts in terms of θ.
- Differentiate to get δx, δy in terms of δθ.
- Sum F·δr, set it to zero and solve.

Worked example: two equal light bars AB and BC of length L are pinned together at B. A is pinned to the ground and C sits on a smooth roller on the same level floor; each bar makes angle θ with the horizontal. A vertical load P acts at B and a horizontal force Q at C stops the linkage spreading. Then y_B = L sin θ and x_C = 2L cos θ, so δy_B = L cos θ δθ and δx_C = −2L sin θ δθ. Virtual work: −P(L cos θ δθ) − Q(−2L sin θ δθ) = 0 for any δθ, giving Q = P/(2 tan θ). The pin reactions at A and B and the roller reaction at C never appear.

Potential energy and stability: for conservative forces, δW = −δV, so equilibrium positions satisfy dV/dq = 0. The second derivative tells you the type:
- d²V/dq² > 0: a minimum of V, stable equilibrium.
- d²V/dq² < 0: a maximum, unstable equilibrium.
- d²V/dq² = 0: test higher derivatives (neutral or more subtle behaviour).

Common potential energies:
- Gravity: V = mgh, with h the height of the centre of mass.
- Linear spring: V = ½kx², with x the extension or compression from the natural length.
- Torsional spring: V = ½k_tθ².

Worked stability example: a uniform rod of weight W and length L stands upright on a pin at its base, with a torsional spring k_t that is unstrained when the rod is vertical. With θ measured from the vertical, V = ½k_tθ² + W(L/2)cos θ. Then dV/dθ = k_tθ − (WL/2)sin θ, which is zero at θ = 0, and d²V/dθ² at θ = 0 equals k_t − WL/2. The upright position is stable only if k_t > WL/2. This "spring stiffness versus destabilising gravity" comparison is the basis of buckling and stability analyses met later in structures.

The same variational ideas extend to dynamics through Lagrange's equations; check your lecture notes for how far this module takes them.

Exam tips: always state the constraint that makes a reaction workless before leaving it out; measure heights to the centre of mass; and for stability, evaluate the second derivative at each equilibrium position separately.

Kinematics describes motion without asking what causes it. This note reads the descriptor's title 'Simple motion' as particle kinematics, covering motion in a straight line, projectiles, circular motion and motion described in polar coordinates.

Straight-line motion:
- v = dx/dt and a = dv/dt = d²x/dt².
- Also a = v dv/dx, which is the form to use when acceleration is given as a function of position.
- Areas under graphs: displacement is the area under a v–t graph; change in velocity is the area under an a–t graph.

Constant acceleration only (the "suvat" equations):
- v = u + at
- s = ut + ½at²
- v² = u² + 2as
- s = ½(u + v)t

When acceleration varies, integrate:
- a given as a(t): integrate directly in time.
- a given as a(v): separate to dt = dv/a(v).
- a given as a(x): use v dv = a(x) dx.

Worked example: a body moving at 10 m/s decelerates with a = −0.5v (SI units). Then dv/dt = −0.5v gives v = 10e^(−0.5t), so v = 3.68 m/s after 2 s. Using v dv/dx = −0.5v gives dv/dx = −0.5, so the body travels 20 m before (asymptotically) stopping.

Projectiles (uniform gravity, no air resistance), launched at speed u and angle α above the horizontal:
- x = (u cos α)t, y = (u sin α)t − ½gt².
- Time of flight on level ground: 2u sin α/g.
- Maximum height: H = u² sin²α/(2g).
- Range on level ground: R = u² sin 2α/g, greatest at α = 45°.
For u = 50 m/s and α = 30°: time of flight 5.10 s, H = 31.9 m, R = 221 m.

Circular motion at radius r:
- Speed v = rω, where ω = dθ/dt.
- Tangential acceleration a_t = dv/dt = rα (α = dω/dt).
- Normal (centripetal) acceleration a_n = v²/r = rω², directed towards the centre. A particle at constant speed on a circle is still accelerating.

Normal–tangential components for any curved path: a = (dv/dt) e_t + (v²/ρ) e_n, where ρ is the local radius of curvature.

Polar coordinates (r, θ), useful when a distance and an angle are measured, such as a radar tracking an aircraft or a slider on a rotating arm:
- v = ṙ e_r + rθ̇ e_θ
- a = (r̈ − rθ̇²) e_r + (rθ̈ + 2ṙθ̇) e_θ
- −rθ̇² is the centripetal term; 2ṙθ̇ is the Coriolis term, present whenever r and θ change together.

Relative motion (translating frames): r_B = r_A + r_B/A, so v_B = v_A + v_B/A and a_B = a_A + a_B/A. This is how you handle problems such as wind relative to an aircraft or one vehicle observed from another.

Exam tips: check whether acceleration is constant before using suvat; choose the coordinate system that matches the measurements given; and never drop the Coriolis term in polar problems just because θ̈ = 0.

notes.h: Particle dynamics: Newton's laws in action
notes.body:
Particle dynamics links forces to motion. A body can be treated as a particle when its rotation does not matter, so all forces can be taken to act at the centre of mass.

Newton's laws:
- First: a body remains at rest or in uniform straight-line motion unless a net force acts.
- Second: ΣF = ma, valid in an inertial (non-accelerating, non-rotating) frame. More generally ΣF = d(mv)/dt.
- Third: forces between two bodies are equal in size, opposite in direction and collinear.

Method for every problem:
- Draw a free body diagram with all external forces (weight mg, normal reactions, friction, tensions, drag).
- Draw the matching kinetic diagram showing ma (in components).
- Choose axes that fit the motion: Cartesian for straight lines, normal–tangential for known curved paths, polar for rotating arms or tracking problems.
- Write ΣF = ma in each direction and add kinematic constraints (such as string length).

Component forms:
- Normal–tangential: ΣF_t = m dv/dt and ΣF_n = mv²/ρ (towards the centre of curvature).
- Polar: ΣF_r = m(r̈ − rθ̇²) and ΣF_θ = m(rθ̈ + 2ṙθ̇).

Connected particles: for two masses m₁ < m₂ hanging over a light, smooth pulley on a light inextensible string (an Atwood machine), the string gives both the same magnitude of acceleration. Then a = (m₂ − m₁)g/(m₁ + m₂) and T = 2m₁m₂g/(m₁ + m₂). With m₁ = 3 kg and m₂ = 5 kg: a = 2.45 m/s² and T = 36.8 N, which sits between the two weights (29.4 N and 49.1 N), as it must.

Banked curves: a vehicle rounding a frictionless bank of angle θ at radius r needs N sin θ = mv²/r and N cos θ = mg, so tan θ = v²/(rg). For v = 20 m/s and r = 100 m, θ = 22.2°.

Losing contact: a car over a hump of radius r has N = m(g − v²/r) at the top. Contact is lost when N = 0, i.e. v = √(gr).

Resisted motion: with linear drag F = −cv, falling from rest gives m dv/dt = mg − cv, so v → mg/c (terminal velocity) exponentially. With quadratic drag F = −cv², terminal velocity is √(mg/c). Quadratic drag is the better model for most aerodynamic bodies at engineering speeds.

Systems of particles: summing Newton's second law over all particles, internal forces cancel in pairs (third law), leaving ΣF_ext = M a_G. The centre of mass moves as if all the mass and all the external forces were concentrated there. This is what justifies treating an aircraft as a point mass in performance calculations.

Non-inertial frames: in an accelerating frame you must add fictitious forces (such as −ma_frame) to use ΣF = ma. For most first-year problems, work in an inertial frame and avoid this.

Exam tips: never put "ma" on the free body diagram as a force; keep the sign convention consistent between FBD and kinetic diagram; and check limiting cases (equal masses give a = 0; θ = 0 gives no banking).

Vibration matters greatly in aerospace: wings flex, engines excite airframes and structural resonance must be avoided. The basic model is the single-degree-of-freedom (SDOF) mass–spring–damper.

Equation of motion: m ẍ + c ẋ + k x = F(t), where m is mass, c the viscous damping coefficient and k the spring stiffness, with x measured from static equilibrium (so gravity drops out for a vertical spring).

Free undamped vibration (c = 0, F = 0):
- ẍ + ωₙ²x = 0 with natural frequency ωₙ = √(k/m) in rad/s.
- Solution x = A cos ωₙt + B sin ωₙt: simple harmonic motion.
- Frequency in hertz fₙ = ωₙ/(2π); period T = 1/fₙ.
- Example: m = 2 kg, k = 800 N/m gives ωₙ = 20 rad/s, fₙ = 3.18 Hz.
- For a vertical spring, ωₙ = √(g/δ_st), where δ_st is the static deflection.

Free damped vibration:
- Damping ratio ζ = c/c_c, with critical damping c_c = 2√(km) = 2mωₙ.
- ζ < 1 (underdamped): x = Xe^(−ζωₙt) cos(ω_d t − φ), oscillating at the damped natural frequency ω_d = ωₙ√(1 − ζ²).
- ζ = 1 (critically damped): returns to rest fastest without overshoot.
- ζ > 1 (overdamped): slow return with no oscillation.
- Logarithmic decrement from two successive peaks: δ = ln(x₁/x₂) = 2πζ/√(1 − ζ²), so ζ = δ/√(4π² + δ²). For light damping, ζ ≈ δ/(2π).
- Example: m = 2 kg, k = 800 N/m, c = 16 N s/m gives c_c = 80 N s/m, ζ = 0.2 and ω_d = 19.6 rad/s.

Forced vibration with F = F₀ cos ωt:
- After the transient dies away, the steady response is x = X cos(ωt − φ).
- With frequency ratio r = ω/ωₙ and static deflection x_st = F₀/k:
- X/x_st = 1/√((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²)
- tan φ = 2ζr/(1 − r²)
- At r = 1 (resonance) the magnification is 1/(2ζ) and the response lags the force by 90°.
- The peak of the amplitude curve is at r = √(1 − 2ζ²), slightly below 1, when ζ < 1/√2.
- Well above resonance (r ≫ 1) the response is small and nearly 180° out of phase: the mass is "inertia controlled".

Energy view: for undamped SHM, kinetic and strain energy exchange, with ½kX² = ½m(ωₙX)², which gives another quick route to ωₙ (Rayleigh's method).

Equivalent springs: springs in parallel add (k = k₁ + k₂); in series the compliances add (1/k = 1/k₁ + 1/k₂).

Exam tips: keep rad/s and Hz apart (divide by 2π to get hertz); quote ζ as a pure number; check that X/x_st tends to 1 as r → 0; and when asked for "natural frequency" of a damped system, say whether you mean ωₙ or ω_d.

Integrating Newton's second law over distance gives energy methods; integrating over time gives momentum methods. Both avoid solving for accelerations and are often far quicker.

Work and energy:
- Work done by a force: U = ∫F·dr. Only the component along the motion does work; normal reactions on a fixed smooth surface do none.
- Kinetic energy: T = ½mv² (particle); ½Iω² for rotation about a fixed axis; ½mv_G² + ½I_Gω² for a rigid body in plane motion.
- Work–energy principle: U₁→₂ = T₂ − T₁.
- Conservative forces (gravity, springs) have potential energies (mgh, ½kx²) and do work independent of path. If only conservative forces do work, T + V is constant.
- Non-conservative forces (friction, drag) remove mechanical energy: T₁ + V₁ + U_nc = T₂ + V₂.
- Power: P = F·v (and P = Mω for a torque), the rate of doing work.

Worked example: a 0.5 kg block is released from a spring (k = 2000 N/m) compressed by 0.1 m on a smooth surface. Strain energy ½kx² = 10 J becomes kinetic energy, so v = √(2 × 10/0.5) = 6.32 m/s. If it then runs up a smooth slope it rises h = 10/(0.5 × 9.81) = 2.04 m, whatever the slope angle.

Impulse and momentum:
- Linear momentum p = mv; impulse ∫F dt = Δp.
- If the net external impulse on a system is zero (or negligible during a short impact), total momentum is conserved.
- Angular momentum about a fixed point O: h_O = r × mv; ΣM_O = dh_O/dt. If the moment about O is zero (central forces), h_O is conserved. That is the basis of Kepler's second law in orbital mechanics.
- For a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis, h = Iω, so a change in I at zero external moment changes ω (a spinning skater pulling in their arms).

Direct central impact:
- Conservation of momentum: m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂.
- Newton's law of restitution: v₂ − v₁ = e(u₁ − u₂), with 0 ≤ e ≤ 1.
- e = 1 is perfectly elastic (kinetic energy conserved); e = 0 is perfectly plastic (bodies move together).
- Worked example: 2 kg at 4 m/s hits a stationary 3 kg body with e = 0.5. Momentum: 8 = 2v₁ + 3v₂; restitution: v₂ − v₁ = 2. So v₁ = 0.4 m/s and v₂ = 2.4 m/s. Kinetic energy falls from 16 J to 8.8 J, so 7.2 J is lost (to heat, sound and deformation).

Variable mass (rockets): applying momentum to a system that ejects mass leads to the thrust term ṁu_e and, with no gravity or drag, to the rocket equation Δv = u_e ln(m₀/m_f). This links directly to orbital manoeuvres.

Choosing a method:
- Forces known as functions of position, speeds wanted: use energy.
- Forces known as functions of time, or impacts: use impulse–momentum.
- Accelerations or forces at an instant: use Newton's second law directly.

Exam tips: say which bodies make up your system before writing a conservation law; remember that momentum can be conserved while energy is lost; and check signs of velocities in impact problems by drawing before-and-after sketches.

notes.h: Orbital mechanics: motion under a central force
notes.body:
Orbital mechanics applies particle dynamics to a body moving under gravity alone. For a small satellite around Earth, Newton's law of gravitation gives an acceleration of magnitude μ/r² towards Earth's centre, where μ = GM ≈ 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s² for Earth.

Central force consequences:
- The force always points to the centre, so its moment about the centre is zero and the specific angular momentum h = r × v is constant. The orbit lies in a fixed plane.
- In polar form h = r²θ̇, so the radius sweeps out area at a constant rate. This is Kepler's second law (equal areas in equal times).
- Gravity is conservative, so the specific energy ε = v²/2 − μ/r is constant.

Orbit shapes: solving the equation of motion gives a conic section, r = (h²/μ)/(1 + e cos θ), with the attracting body at a focus. Eccentricity e = 0 gives a circle, 0 < e < 1 an ellipse (Kepler's first law), e = 1 a parabola and e > 1 a hyperbola.

Key results for ellipses with semi-major axis a:
- Energy: ε = −μ/(2a), so a depends only on energy.
- Vis-viva equation: v² = μ(2/r − 1/a), the speed at any radius.
- Period: T = 2π√(a³/μ), so T² ∝ a³ (Kepler's third law).
- Periapsis and apoapsis radii: r_p = a(1 − e), r_a = a(1 + e).

Circular orbits (r = a):
- Speed v_c = √(μ/r). Period T = 2π√(r³/μ).
- Example: at 400 km altitude (r = 6371 + 400 = 6771 km), v_c ≈ 7.67 km/s and T ≈ 92.4 min.
- Geostationary orbit: the period equals one sidereal day (about 86 164 s), giving r ≈ 42 164 km, about 35 786 km above the equator.

Escape: setting ε = 0 gives the escape speed v_esc = √(2μ/r) = √2 × v_c. From the 400 km orbit, v_esc ≈ 10.85 km/s, so an extra 3.18 km/s is needed.

Hohmann transfer: the standard two-impulse transfer between coplanar circular orbits of radii r₁ and r₂ uses an ellipse with periapsis r₁ and apoapsis r₂, so a_t = (r₁ + r₂)/2.
- First burn at r₁: Δv₁ = √(μ(2/r₁ − 1/a_t)) − √(μ/r₁).
- Second burn at r₂: Δv₂ = √(μ/r₂) − √(μ(2/r₂ − 1/a_t)).
- Transfer time: half the ellipse period, π√(a_t³/μ).
- From 400 km altitude to geostationary radius: Δv₁ ≈ 2.40 km/s, Δv₂ ≈ 1.46 km/s, total about 3.86 km/s (ignoring the plane change usually also needed), taking about 5.3 h.

Physical points worth remembering:
- Lower orbits are faster: v_c falls as r increases.
- To raise an orbit you speed up (prograde burn), yet the final circular speed is lower, because the satellite climbs against gravity.
- The velocity changes (Δv) needed are linked to propellant by the rocket equation Δv = u_e ln(m₀/m_f).

Exam tips: use r measured from Earth's centre, never altitude, in every formula; keep units in metres and seconds; and quote whether a speed is circular, transfer-orbit or escape speed.

cards.f: Cross product a × b in components
cards.b: (a_yb_z − a_zb_y, a_zbₓ − aₓb_z, aₓb_y − a_ybₓ). Reversing the order changes the sign: b × a = −(a × b).

cards.f: Moment of a force about a point O
cards.b: M_O = r × F, where r is the position vector from O to any point on the force's line of action.

cards.f: Moment of a force about an axis
cards.b: M_n = n·(r × F), where n is a unit vector along the axis and r runs from a point on the axis to the line of action.
I = I_G + md², where I_G is about a parallel axis through the centre of mass G and d is the distance between the two axes.
Axis perpendicular to the rod: mL²/12 through the centre; mL²/3 through one end.
The distance k such that I = mk²: the radius at which all the mass could be concentrated to give the same moment of inertia.
For a flat lamina in the xy-plane, I_z = Iₓ + I_y, where z is perpendicular to the lamina. It does not apply to 3D bodies.
Axes about which all products of inertia are zero, so the inertia tensor is diagonal. For symmetric bodies they lie along the axes of symmetry.

cards.f: Equilibrium equations for a rigid body in 3D
cards.b: ΣF = 0 and ΣM = 0 about any point: six independent scalar equations (three force, three moment). In 2D there are three.
No slip: F ≤ μ_s N. Impending slip: F = μ_s N. Sliding: F = μ_k N, opposing relative motion. Usually μ_k < μ_s.
φ with tan φ = μ_s. A block on an incline is on the point of slipping when the slope angle equals φ.
T₂/T₁ = e^(μβ) at impending slip, with T₂ the tight-side tension, μ the friction coefficient and β the wrap angle in radians.

cards.f: Force in a cable from A to B
cards.b: T = T(r_B − r_A)/|r_B − r_A|: the tension magnitude times the unit vector pointing along the cable from the body towards the anchor.
A member loaded only at two points (e.g. a pin-ended light strut). For equilibrium the two forces are equal, opposite and act along the line joining the points.
A body in equilibrium under three non-parallel forces: their lines of action must meet at a single point (concurrency).
Unknown reactions equal the number of independent equilibrium equations and the supports properly restrain the body, so statics alone gives all reactions.
An imagined, infinitesimal change of configuration that respects the constraints, taken with time held fixed.
With ideal (workless) constraints, a system is in equilibrium if and only if the virtual work of the applied forces is zero for every admissible virtual displacement.

cards.f: Why do ideal support reactions drop out of virtual work?
cards.b: Frictionless pins, smooth contacts and inextensible links do no work in any displacement the constraints allow, so their virtual work is zero.
For one generalised coordinate q, the quantity Q in δW = Q δq. Equilibrium requires Q = 0.
For conservative systems equilibrium occurs where dV/dq = 0.
d²V/dq² > 0: stable (minimum of V). d²V/dq² < 0: unstable (maximum). Zero: check higher derivatives.

cards.f: Potential energy of a linear spring
cards.b: V = ½kx², where x is the extension or compression from the natural length (not from some other datum).

cards.f: Acceleration as a function of position
cards.b: Use a = v dv/dx, so v dv = a(x) dx, then integrate.

cards.f: When do the suvat equations apply?
cards.b: Only for straight-line motion (or each Cartesian component) with constant acceleration.
R = u² sin 2α/g (no air resistance). It is greatest at α = 45°.
H = u² sin²α/(2g), reached at time u sin α/g.
a_n = v²/r = rω², directed towards the centre of the circle, even when the speed is constant.
a = (r̈ − rθ̇²) e_r + (rθ̈ + 2ṙθ̇) e_θ.
2ṙθ̇ in the transverse acceleration: it appears whenever the radius and angle change at the same time.
v_B = v_A + v_B/A: velocity of B equals velocity of A plus velocity of B relative to A (translating frames).
ΣF = ma (more generally ΣF = d(mv)/dt), valid in an inertial frame.
a = (m₂ − m₁)g/(m₁ + m₂) for masses on a light inextensible string over a smooth light pulley.
T = 2m₁m₂g/(m₁ + m₂), which always lies between the two weights.
tan θ = v²/(rg): the horizontal component of the normal force supplies the centripetal force.

cards.f: Car over a hump: when is contact lost?
cards.b: At the top N = m(g − v²/r); contact is lost when N = 0, i.e. v = √(gr).
m dv/dt = mg − cv gives v_terminal = mg/c. With quadratic drag cv², v_terminal = √(mg/c).

cards.f: Motion of the centre of mass
cards.b: ΣF_ext = M a_G: internal forces cancel in pairs, so G moves as a particle carrying all the mass and external forces.
ωₙ = √(k/m) rad/s; fₙ = ωₙ/(2π) Hz.
c_c = 2√(km) = 2mωₙ. Damping ratio ζ = c/c_c.
ω_d = ωₙ√(1 − ζ²), defined for underdamped systems (ζ < 1).
δ = ln(x₁/x₂) for successive peaks = 2πζ/√(1 − ζ²), so ζ = δ/√(4π² + δ²).
X/x_st = 1/√((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²), with r = ω/ωₙ and x_st = F₀/k.
Magnification 1/(2ζ) and the displacement lags the force by 90°.
Parallel: k = k₁ + k₂. Series: 1/k = 1/k₁ + 1/k₂.
For a mass on a vertical spring, ωₙ = √(g/δ_st), since k δ_st = mg.
The work done by all forces on a body equals its change in kinetic energy: U₁→₂ = T₂ − T₁.
If only conservative forces do work, T + V is constant; non-conservative work (friction, drag) changes T + V.
∫F dt = Δ(mv): the impulse of the net force equals the change in linear momentum.
e = (v₂ − v₁)/(u₁ − u₂): separation speed over approach speed along the line of impact. e = 1 elastic, e = 0 perfectly plastic.

cards.f: Kinetic energy of a rigid body in plane motion
cards.b: T = ½mv_G² + ½I_Gω²: translation of the centre of mass plus rotation about it.
If the net moment of external forces about a fixed point O is zero, h_O = r × mv is constant.
P = F·v for a force, P = Mω for a torque: the rate of doing work, in watts.
Δv = u_e ln(m₀/m_f), where u_e is the exhaust speed relative to the rocket, with no gravity or drag.
v_c = √(μ/r), with r measured from the centre of the attracting body.
v² = μ(2/r − 1/a): speed at radius r on a conic orbit of semi-major axis a.
T = 2π√(a³/μ), so T² ∝ a³ (Kepler's third law).
v_esc = √(2μ/r) = √2 × circular speed at the same radius; specific energy is zero.
A line from the central body to the satellite sweeps equal areas in equal times; it follows from conservation of angular momentum.
ε = v²/2 − μ/r = −μ/(2a): negative for closed (elliptical) orbits, zero for parabolic escape.
Two-impulse transfer between coplanar circular orbits along an ellipse tangent to both, with a = (r₁ + r₂)/2; transfer time is half its period.
Period of one sidereal day (about 86 164 s) gives r ≈ 42 164 km from Earth's centre, about 35 786 km above the equator.

questions.q: A uniform slender rod of mass 2 kg and length 1.5 m rotates about an axis through one end, perpendicular to the rod. What is its moment of inertia about this axis?
questions.why: About an end, I = mL²/3 = 2 × 1.5²/3 = 1.5 kg m² (equivalently mL²/12 + m(L/2)²). 0.375 kg m² is mL²/12, the value about the centre, so the axis shift has been ignored. 4.5 kg m² is mL², which treats all the mass as if it sat at the far end. 4.875 kg m² comes from applying the parallel axis theorem with d = L instead of d = L/2.

questions.q: A force F = (2, −1, 3) N acts through the point r = (1, 2, 0) m. What is its moment about the origin?
questions.why: M = r × F = (2×3 − 0×(−1), 0×2 − 1×3, 1×(−1) − 2×2) = (6, −3, −5) N m. (−6, 3, 5) N m is F × r, the cross product taken in the wrong order. (2, −2, 0) N m multiplies matching components together, which is not a cross product at all. (6, 3, −5) N m comes from writing the middle component as aₓb_z − a_zbₓ, the reverse of the correct a_zbₓ − aₓb_z.

questions.q: A uniform thin disc has mass 4 kg and radius 0.3 m. Find its moment of inertia (a) about the axis through its centre perpendicular to its plane and (b) about a parallel axis through a point on its rim. Hence find the radius of gyration about the rim axis.
markScheme: Parallel axis theorem with d = R: I = I_G + mR²
questions.modelAnswer: (a) For a uniform disc about its central axis, I_G = mR²/2 = 0.5 × 4 × 0.3² = 0.18 kg m². (b) The rim axis is parallel and a distance R = 0.3 m away, so I = I_G + mR² = 0.18 + 4 × 0.09 = 0.54 kg m² (that is, 3mR²/2). Radius of gyration: k = √(I/m) = √(0.54/4) = √0.135 ≈ 0.367 m.

questions.q: A 50 kg crate rests on a slope at 20° to the horizontal, with μ_s = 0.4 (g = 9.81 m/s²). What force, applied parallel to the slope, is needed to start the crate moving up the slope?
questions.why: Moving up, friction acts down the slope at its limit: P = mg(sin 20° + 0.4 cos 20°) = 490.5 × (0.342 + 0.376) ≈ 352 N. 168 N is just mg sin 20°, the weight component, with friction ignored. About 17 N is mg(0.4 cos 20° − sin 20°), the force needed to start the crate sliding down the slope, not up it. 528 N is mg(cos 20° + 0.4 sin 20°), which swaps sine and cosine.

questions.q: A block rests on a rough plank whose angle can be slowly increased. The coefficient of static friction is 0.5. At what angle does the block start to slip?
questions.why: Slip begins when mg sin θ = μ_s mg cos θ, i.e. tan θ = μ_s = 0.5, so θ = 26.6°. 30.0° would need sin θ = 0.5, which equates friction coefficient with sin θ instead of tan θ. 60.0° comes from setting cos θ = 0.5. 63.4° comes from tan θ = 1/μ_s = 2, which inverts the ratio.

questions.q: A rope is wrapped one and a half turns round a fixed bollard (μ = 0.3). The load side carries 5000 N. What is the smallest pull on the free end that will stop the rope slipping?
markScheme: Capstan equation T₂/T₁ = e^(μβ), with T₂ = 5000 N the tight (load) side
questions.modelAnswer: The wrap angle is 1.5 turns = 3π rad. At impending slip the capstan equation gives T₂/T₁ = e^(μβ) = e^(0.3 × 3π) = e^(2.83) ≈ 16.9. The load side is the tight side, T₂ = 5000 N, so the holding force is T₁ = 5000/16.9 ≈ 296 N. Any pull at least this large prevents slipping.

questions.q: A uniform rod of weight W = 300 N and length L = 0.8 m stands vertically on a pin at its lower end. A torsional spring at the pin is unstrained when the rod is vertical. What is the smallest spring stiffness for which the vertical position is stable?
questions.why: V = ½k_tθ² + W(L/2)cos θ, so d²V/dθ² at θ = 0 is k_t − WL/2. Stability needs k_t > WL/2 = 300 × 0.4 = 120 N m/rad. 240 N m/rad is WL, which puts the weight at the top of the rod instead of at its centre of mass. 60 N m/rad is WL/4, halving the lever arm twice. 300 N m/rad is just W with no lever arm, so it is not even dimensionally a moment.

questions.q: When writing a virtual work equation for a mechanism, which forces can be left out?
options: Friction forces at a sliding contact, because they are contact reactions
Spring forces, because springs store energy rather than dissipate it
Reactions at frictionless pins and smooth supports
Weights of the members, because gravity is conservative
questions.why: Ideal constraints (frictionless pins, smooth contacts) do no work in any admissible virtual displacement, so their reactions vanish from the equation. Weights must be included: being conservative just means they can be written as −δV, not that they do no work. Friction at a sliding contact does work during the displacement, so it is not a workless constraint. Spring forces also do virtual work; storing energy is exactly why they appear, through the change in ½kx².

questions.q: A one-degree-of-freedom system has potential energy V(x) = x³ − 3x (V in J, x in m). Find the equilibrium positions and state whether each is stable or unstable.
markScheme: Equilibria at x = +1 m and x = −1 m
questions.modelAnswer: Equilibrium requires dV/dx = 3x² − 3 = 0, so x = ±1 m. The second derivative is d²V/dx² = 6x. At x = +1 m it is +6 > 0, a local minimum of V, so the equilibrium is stable. At x = −1 m it is −6 < 0, a local maximum, so the equilibrium is unstable.

questions.q: A projectile is launched from level ground at 50 m/s, 30° above the horizontal (g = 9.81 m/s², no air resistance). How far away does it land?
questions.why: R = u² sin 2α/g = 2500 × sin 60°/9.81 ≈ 221 m. 110 m is u² sin α cos α/g, which drops the factor 2 in sin 2α = 2 sin α cos α. 255 m multiplies the full launch speed by the time of flight (50 × 5.10 s), forgetting to take the horizontal component u cos α. 31.9 m is the maximum height u² sin²α/(2g), not the range.

questions.q: A slider moves along a rotating arm. At one instant r = 2 m, ṙ = 1 m/s, r̈ = 0, θ̇ = 3 rad/s and θ̈ = 0. What is the transverse (e_θ) component of its acceleration?
questions.why: a_θ = rθ̈ + 2ṙθ̇ = 0 + 2 × 1 × 3 = 6 m/s². 3 m/s² drops the factor 2 in the Coriolis term. 0 m/s² assumes no transverse acceleration because θ̈ = 0, forgetting the Coriolis term altogether. −18 m/s² is the radial component r̈ − rθ̇² = 0 − 2 × 9, not the transverse one.

questions.q: A body moving in a straight line at 10 m/s experiences an acceleration a = −0.5v (SI units). Find (a) its speed after 2 s and (b) the total distance it travels before coming to rest.
markScheme: Use a = v dv/dx: v dv/dx = −0.5v so dv/dx = −0.5
Integrate from v = 10 to v = 0: x = 10/0.5 = 20 m
Notes that v → 0 only as t → ∞ but the distance is finite
questions.modelAnswer: (a) dv/dt = −0.5v. Separating, ln(v/10) = −0.5t, so v = 10e^(−0.5t). After 2 s, v = 10e^(−1) ≈ 3.68 m/s. (b) Writing a = v dv/dx gives v dv/dx = −0.5v, so dv/dx = −0.5 and v = 10 − 0.5x. The speed reaches zero at x = 20 m. In time the speed only tends to zero as t → ∞, but the distance covered approaches a finite 20 m.

questions.q: Masses of 3 kg and 5 kg hang on either side of a light, smooth pulley, joined by a light inextensible string. What is the tension in the string? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
questions.why: a = (5 − 3)g/8 = 2.45 m/s², and T = 3(g + a) = 2m₁m₂g/(m₁ + m₂) = 36.8 N. 29.4 N is the weight of the 3 kg mass, which would only be the tension if nothing accelerated. 49.1 N is the weight of the 5 kg mass, the same static mistake on the other side. 19.6 N is (m₂ − m₁)g, the net driving weight that accelerates the system, not the string tension.

questions.q: A road curve of radius 100 m is to be banked so that cars at 20 m/s need no friction. What bank angle is needed? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
questions.why: tan θ = v²/(rg) = 400/981 = 0.408, so θ = 22.2°. 1.2° uses v instead of v² in the formula. 24.1° comes from sin θ = v²/(rg), which wrongly takes the normal force as N = mg instead of using N cos θ = mg. 67.8° is the complement, from tan θ = rg/v², i.e. the ratio inverted.

questions.q: A car drives over a hump-backed bridge whose top is a circular arc of radius 40 m. Find the greatest speed at which the car stays in contact with the road at the top. (g = 9.81 m/s²)
markScheme: At the top, weight minus normal force provides centripetal force: mg − N = mv²/r
questions.modelAnswer: At the top of the hump the net downward force provides the centripetal acceleration: mg − N = mv²/r, so N = m(g − v²/r). The car stays in contact while N ≥ 0, so the limit is v² = gr. With r = 40 m, v = √(9.81 × 40) ≈ 19.8 m/s, about 71 km/h. The mass cancels, so the answer is the same for any car.

questions.q: A 2 kg mass is supported by a spring of stiffness 800 N/m. What is its undamped natural frequency in hertz?
questions.why: ωₙ = √(k/m) = √400 = 20 rad/s, so fₙ = 20/(2π) = 3.18 Hz. 20 Hz is the angular frequency in rad/s quoted as if it were hertz. 63.7 Hz is (k/m)/(2π) = 400/(2π), which forgets the square root. 126 Hz multiplies 20 rad/s by 2π instead of dividing.

questions.q: A system has m = 2 kg, k = 800 N/m and viscous damping c = 16 N s/m. What is the damping ratio ζ?
questions.why: c_c = 2√(km) = 2√1600 = 80 N s/m, so ζ = 16/80 = 0.2. 0.02 is c/k, which is not dimensionless and is not the damping ratio. 0.4 is c/√(km), missing the factor 2 in the critical damping coefficient. 4.0 is c/(2m) = ζωₙ, the exponential decay rate in s⁻¹, not a ratio.

questions.q: In a free-vibration test two successive displacement peaks are 10 mm and 6 mm. Find the logarithmic decrement and the damping ratio, and comment on whether the light-damping approximation is adequate.
markScheme: Light-damping approximation ζ ≈ δ/(2π) ≈ 0.0813, within about 0.3%, so adequate
questions.modelAnswer: The logarithmic decrement is δ = ln(x₁/x₂) = ln(10/6) = 0.511. The exact relation ζ = δ/√(4π² + δ²) gives ζ = 0.511/√(39.48 + 0.26) ≈ 0.0810. The light-damping approximation ζ ≈ δ/(2π) gives 0.0813, which differs by about 0.3%, so it is perfectly adequate at this level of damping.

questions.q: A 2 kg body moving at 4 m/s strikes a stationary 3 kg body head-on. The coefficient of restitution is 0.5. What is the speed of the 3 kg body after the impact?
questions.why: Momentum gives 8 = 2v₁ + 3v₂ and restitution gives v₂ − v₁ = 0.5 × 4 = 2, so v₁ = 0.4 m/s and v₂ = 2.4 m/s. 1.6 m/s is the common speed for a perfectly plastic impact (e = 0). 3.2 m/s is the result for a perfectly elastic impact (e = 1). 2.0 m/s is the separation speed e(u₁ − u₂), not the speed of either body.

questions.q: For the same impact (2 kg at 4 m/s hitting a stationary 3 kg body, e = 0.5), how much kinetic energy is lost?
questions.why: Before: ½ × 2 × 4² = 16 J. After: ½ × 2 × 0.4² + ½ × 3 × 2.4² = 0.16 + 8.64 = 8.8 J. The loss is 16 − 8.8 = 7.2 J. 8.8 J is the kinetic energy remaining, not the amount lost. 9.6 J is the loss for a perfectly plastic impact (16 − 6.4). 0 J wrongly assumes that conserving momentum also conserves kinetic energy, which is only true when e = 1.

questions.q: A 0.5 kg block on a smooth horizontal surface is pressed against a spring (k = 2000 N/m), compressing it by 0.1 m, and released. Find its speed after leaving the spring and the height it reaches up a smooth ramp. (g = 9.81 m/s²)
markScheme: All converted to kinetic energy: ½mv² = 10 J
At the top all kinetic energy becomes mgh: h = 10/(0.5 × 9.81) ≈ 2.04 m, independent of ramp angle
questions.modelAnswer: The spring stores ½kx² = ½ × 2000 × 0.01 = 10 J. With no friction this all becomes kinetic energy: ½ × 0.5 × v² = 10, so v = √40 ≈ 6.32 m/s. On a smooth ramp the block climbs until its kinetic energy has all become potential energy: mgh = 10 J, so h = 10/(0.5 × 9.81) ≈ 2.04 m. Because the normal force does no work, the height does not depend on the ramp angle.

questions.q: What is the speed of a satellite in a circular orbit 400 km above Earth's surface? (μ = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s², Earth radius 6371 km)
questions.why: v = √(μ/r) with r = 6771 km gives 7.67 km/s. 10.85 km/s is √(2μ/r), the escape speed at that radius. 7.91 km/s uses Earth's radius (6371 km) as r, ignoring the altitude. 31.6 km/s uses the altitude (400 km) as r instead of the distance from Earth's centre.

questions.q: Kepler's second law (equal areas swept in equal times) is a direct consequence of which principle?
options: The period–semi-major axis relation T² ∝ a³
Conservation of linear momentum of the satellite
Conservation of angular momentum about the central body
questions.why: Gravity is a central force with zero moment about the attracting body, so h = r²θ̇ is constant, and the areal rate h/2 is constant. Energy conservation fixes the size of the orbit (through a) but not the rate of sweeping area. T² ∝ a³ is Kepler's third law, a different result. The satellite's linear momentum is not conserved: gravity continually changes its direction.

questions.q: Using μ = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s², find (a) the period of a circular orbit 400 km above Earth's surface (Earth radius 6371 km) and (b) the radius of a geostationary orbit, taking the sidereal day as 86 164 s.
markScheme: r = 6.771 × 10⁶ m (radius from Earth's centre, not altitude)
questions.modelAnswer: (a) r = 6371 + 400 = 6771 km = 6.771 × 10⁶ m. T = 2π√(r³/μ) = 2π√((6.771 × 10⁶)³/3.986 × 10¹⁴) ≈ 5545 s ≈ 92.4 min. (b) For a geostationary orbit, T must equal one sidereal day, 86 164 s. Rearranging, r = (μT²/4π²)^(1/3) = (3.986 × 10¹⁴ × 86 164²/(4π²))^(1/3) ≈ 4.216 × 10⁷ m, i.e. about 42 164 km from Earth's centre, roughly 35 786 km above the equator.

questions.q:
A machine component is modelled as a single-degree-of-freedom system with mass m = 2 kg, spring stiffness k = 800 N/m and viscous damping c = 16 N s/m.
(a) Write the equation of motion for a harmonic force F₀ cos ωt and find ωₙ, ζ and ω_d. [6]
(b) The system is released from a displaced position with no force applied. By what factor does the amplitude fall in each cycle, and after how many cycles has it halved? [5]
(c) A force of amplitude F₀ = 40 N is applied at ω = 15 rad/s. Find the steady-state amplitude and the phase lag. [6]
(d) Without further calculation of the full curve, state the frequency at which the steady-state amplitude is greatest and explain briefly why it is not exactly ωₙ. [3]
markScheme: (a) m ẍ + c ẋ + k x = F₀ cos ωt; ωₙ = √(k/m) = 20 rad/s
(b) δ = 2πζ/√(1 − ζ²) ≈ 1.28; amplitude ratio per cycle e^(−δ) ≈ 0.277
(b) cycles to halve n = ln 2/δ ≈ 0.54 (amplitude halves within the first cycle)
(d) peak at r = √(1 − 2ζ²) ≈ 0.959, ω ≈ 19.2 rad/s; damping shifts the peak below ωₙ
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Newton's second law for the mass gives m ẍ + c ẋ + k x = F₀ cos ωt, with x measured from static equilibrium. ωₙ = √(k/m) = √(800/2) = 20 rad/s (3.18 Hz). Critical damping c_c = 2√(km) = 2√1600 = 80 N s/m, so ζ = c/c_c = 16/80 = 0.2. The damped natural frequency is ω_d = 20√(1 − 0.04) ≈ 19.6 rad/s.

(b) The logarithmic decrement is δ = 2πζ/√(1 − ζ²) = 2π(0.2)/0.980 ≈ 1.28. Each cycle the amplitude is multiplied by e^(−δ) ≈ 0.277, i.e. it falls to about 28% of its previous value. The amplitude halves after n cycles where nδ = ln 2, so n ≈ 0.693/1.28 ≈ 0.54 cycles: it has more than halved before the first full cycle is complete.

(c) The static deflection is x_st = F₀/k = 40/800 = 0.05 m and the frequency ratio is r = 15/20 = 0.75. Then 1 − r² = 0.4375 and 2ζr = 0.3, so X = 0.05/√(0.4375² + 0.3²) = 0.05/√(0.1914 + 0.09) = 0.05/0.5305 ≈ 0.0943 m (magnification ≈ 1.89). The phase lag is φ = arctan(0.3/0.4375) ≈ 34.4°, below 90° because the forcing is below resonance.

(d) Differentiating the magnification factor shows the amplitude peak is at r = √(1 − 2ζ²) = √(1 − 0.08) ≈ 0.959, i.e. ω ≈ 19.2 rad/s. It is slightly below ωₙ because damping adds the term (2ζr)² to the denominator, which grows with r and pulls the maximum to a lower frequency. At r = 1 itself the magnification is 1/(2ζ) = 2.5, giving 0.125 m, just below the true peak.

questions.q:
A satellite is in a circular parking orbit 400 km above Earth's surface and is to be transferred to geostationary radius (42 164 km) by a Hohmann transfer. Take μ = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s² and Earth radius 6371 km, and ignore any plane change.
(a) Find the circular speeds in the two orbits and comment on which is faster. [4]
(b) Find the semi-major axis of the transfer ellipse and the speeds at its periapsis and apoapsis. [6]
(c) Find the two velocity increments and the total Δv. [4]
(d) Find the transfer time. [3]
(e) Explain why the satellite must speed up to reach a higher orbit, yet ends up moving more slowly. [3]
markScheme: (a) r₁ = 6771 km, v₁ = √(μ/r₁) ≈ 7.67 km/s; v₂ = √(μ/r₂) ≈ 3.07 km/s; the lower orbit is faster
(c) Δv₁ ≈ 2.40 km/s, Δv₂ ≈ 1.46 km/s, total ≈ 3.86 km/s
(e) Burns add energy (less negative ε = −μ/2a); kinetic energy is traded for potential energy while coasting; circular speed √(μ/r) falls with r
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) r₁ = 6371 + 400 = 6771 km and r₂ = 42 164 km. Circular speeds: v₁ = √(3.986 × 10¹⁴/6.771 × 10⁶) ≈ 7673 m/s and v₂ = √(3.986 × 10¹⁴/4.2164 × 10⁷) ≈ 3075 m/s. The low orbit is more than twice as fast, since v_c ∝ 1/√r.

(b) The transfer ellipse touches both orbits, so a_t = (6771 + 42 164)/2 = 24 467.5 km. By vis-viva, at periapsis v_p = √(μ(2/r₁ − 1/a_t)) ≈ 10 072 m/s and at apoapsis v_a = √(μ(2/r₂ − 1/a_t)) ≈ 1617 m/s. As a check, angular momentum is conserved: r₁v_p = 6.771 × 10⁶ × 10 072 ≈ 6.82 × 10¹⁰ m²/s and r₂v_a = 4.2164 × 10⁷ × 1617 ≈ 6.82 × 10¹⁰ m²/s.

(c) First burn (at r₁, prograde): Δv₁ = 10 072 − 7673 ≈ 2399 m/s. Second burn (at r₂, prograde, to circularise): Δv₂ = 3075 − 1617 ≈ 1457 m/s. Total Δv ≈ 3857 m/s, about 3.86 km/s. In practice a launch from a non-equatorial site also needs a plane change, which adds to this.

(d) The transfer covers half the ellipse: t = π√(a_t³/μ) = π√((2.44675 × 10⁷)³/3.986 × 10¹⁴) ≈ 1.90 × 10⁴ s ≈ 5.3 hours.

(e) Each prograde burn increases the specific energy ε = −μ/(2a), making it less negative and so increasing a. Between burns the satellite coasts outward and trades kinetic energy for gravitational potential energy, slowing from 10.07 km/s to 1.62 km/s. The second burn raises the speed to the local circular value, but that value, √(μ/r₂) ≈ 3.07 km/s, is lower than at r₁ because gravity is weaker further out. Total energy is higher in the final orbit even though speed is lower.
